content:
Listening to faint waves from old hydrogen

Neutral hydrogen gas emits a subtle radio signature at a rest wavelength of 21 centimeters. As the universe expands, ancient radio waves stretch to longer wavelengths before reaching Earth.

The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment, known as CHIME, detects radio waves from 400 to 800 megahertz. A frequency range that captures redshifted emissions from a period when the universe was around five billion years old.

Researchers analyzed data gathered during 94 nighttime observing runs in 2019. Instead of tracking individual galaxies, CHIME measures total hydrogen emissions across broad sectors of space.

Measuring signals through auto-correlation

Earlier hydrogen mapping projects verified their readings by comparing radio maps against external galaxy surveys. This new analysis relies strictly on auto-correlation, measuring statistical patterns within CHIME’s own radio maps.

Removing the need for outside galaxy catalogs represents a major practical breakthrough for radio astronomy. However, extracting this faint signal presents an immense technical challenge for calibration teams.

Neutral hydrogen emits a very weak radio signal. Galactic emissions, cosmic sources, and human wireless networks frequently interfere with these observations.

Mapping large structures to test cosmic expansion

Hydrogen intensity mapping allows cosmologists to chart how large-scale structures clustered across early cosmic history. These large gas distributions preserve imprint patterns created by acoustic pressure waves in the early universe.

Scientists use these ancient acoustic patterns as a standard cosmic ruler to track expansion rates over time. Measuring how this cosmic ruler changes helps researchers test theories about the nature of dark energy.

However, this initial detection does not independently calculate dark energy or predict the universe’s eventual end. It simply confirms that CHIME can isolate the necessary hydrogen signals directly from its own observations.

Overcoming noise and instrumental limits

The 2019 dataset represents only a small fraction of the nearly seven years of data CHIME has gathered. Analyzing the full multiyear archive will yield sharper views of early cosmic structure.

Radio-frequency interference and complex instrument noise still require precise filtering techniques across lower frequency bands. Background noise remains a primary challenge that limits current observational precision.

Future research will focus on refining calibration models and extending observations into earlier cosmic epochs. Astronomers hope to apply these auto-correlation techniques to hydrogen signals emitted when the universe was three billion years old.

What remains uncertain

This study demonstrates that auto-correlation can successfully detect faint 21 centimeter signals across cosmological distances. While the result validates a key observational method, it does not reveal whether dark energy changes over time.

Scientists must still refine foreground removal techniques and replicate these findings across broader observational datasets. Integrating hydrogen maps with existing cosmological models will ultimately help clarify how our expanding universe evolved.

Source: CHIME Collaboration, “Detection of the Cosmological 21 cm Signal in Autocorrelation at z ~ 1 with the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment,” The Astrophysical Journal, 2026.
